name: Lorenzo Lotto
teaser: The uneasy genius of the High Renaissance — a Venetian who never fit in, painting portraits with strange symbols, nervous glances, and psychological tension. His Annunciation shows a startled cat fleeing the angel Gabriel.

exploreAction.targetName: The Annunciation (Recanati) — the cat
exploreAction.instruction: Mary kneels, startled, while the angel hovers at the door — and a terrified cat sprints across the room. Look at the domestic details: the bed, the window, the broom. Lotto painted holy moments as they might actually happen: in a messy room, with a cat.

name: Moretto da Brescia
teaser: The Brescian painter who specialized in silver-grey light and quiet saints — his portraits of armor-clad noblemen and his suave altarpieces made him the leading painter of his city, and his influence reached El Greco.

exploreAction.targetName: Portrait of a Man in Armor or the Assumption altarpiece
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the metallic light: Moretto could paint steel and silk so you feel their weight. His saints stand in calm, luminous rooms, their faces soft and thoughtful. A painter of restraint — everything composed, nothing shouting.

name: Giovanni Girolamo Savoldo
teaser: The Brescian master of twilight and reflection — his shepherds glow in pale night light, and his Magdalens wrapped in silver cloaks are among the most mysterious portraits in Italian art. He painted light that comes from nowhere.

exploreAction.targetName: Mary Magdalene (National Gallery, London) — the cloak
exploreAction.instruction: A woman in a silver-grey cloak stares out from a dark background, her face half-lit. Look at the fabric — it catches light like water. Savoldo's figures always seem to be standing at dusk, just before the light goes. Melancholy, elegance, and mystery.

name: Bernardino Luini
teaser: The Lombard painter who carried Leonardo's sweetness into northern Italy — his Madonnas are gentle, his frescoes are graceful, and his Salome holds the Baptist's head with an expression of mild surprise. He was the most popular 'Leonardo follower.'

exploreAction.targetName: Salome with the Head of John the Baptist (Uffizi) — the face
exploreAction.instruction: Salome presents the severed head on a platter, her face serene, even pretty — the horror is in the mismatch. Look at the soft Leonardo-esque modeling: no harsh lines, just gentle shadow. Luini made even a beheading look polite.

name: Gaudenzio Ferrari
teaser: The Italian painter-sculptor of the Sacro Monte — his fresco cycles in Varallo mix painting and terracotta sculpture into three-dimensional dramas of the life of Christ, with crowds that spill off the walls. He is the cinema of the 16th century.

exploreAction.targetName: The Chapel of the Crucifixion (Sacro Monte, Varallo) — the crowd
exploreAction.instruction: Walk into the chapel: painted soldiers and terracotta figures surround you in a full circle, the crucifixion happening in 3D. Look at how Ferrari fused paint and sculpture so seamlessly you can't tell where one ends. Immersive art, 1530.

name: Bernardo Strozzi
teaser: The Genoese painter known as 'the priest' — he painted kitchens full of cooks and fishwives, saints and allegories, with a Rubens-like energy and a Genoese love of domestic detail. He is the link between Genoa and the Baroque.

exploreAction.targetName: The Cook or The Allegory of Painting (self-portrait)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Cook: a massive woman in white sleeves prepares food, her arms a blur of creamy fabric — a masterpiece of textile painting. Then his self-portrait as the Allegory of Painting: the artist, paintbrush in hand, looking exhausted and triumphant. A priest who painted life in full.

name: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo
teaser: The last great master of the grand Baroque ceiling — his frescoes of sky, gods, and swirling light fill palaces in Venice, Würzburg, and Madrid. He painted air itself; his ceilings seem open to heaven. He is the sunset of the old Italian school.

exploreAction.targetName: The Apollo and the Continents ceiling (Würzburg Residence) — look up
exploreAction.instruction: Tilt your head back: continents, gods, and allegories swirl around a luminous sky, all painted from below in impossible perspective. Look at the pale golds, pinks, and whites — Tiepolo's palette is morning light. He made ceilings into windows.

name: Canaletto
teaser: The Venetian painter who sold Venice to the world — his precise, sunlit views of the Grand Canal, Piazza San Marco, and the Rialto were bought by English tourists by the dozen. He even used a camera obscura to get the perspective exact.

exploreAction.targetName: The Stonemason's Yard (National Gallery, London) — the working Venice
exploreAction.instruction: Most of Canaletto is grand tourist views; this one is different — a working yard near the church of Santa Maria della Carità, with stonemasons, laundry, and children. Look at the light on the walls and the unfinished blocks. The tourist-painter's most human painting.

name: Francesco Guardi
teaser: The Venetian painter of the shimmering, dissolving city — where Canaletto drew buildings, Guardi painted impressions: gondolas, lagoon mist, and festivals dissolving into flickers of paint. He is the Impressionist before Impressionism.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lagoon with Gondolas or the View of San Giorgio Maggiore
exploreAction.instruction: Look at how Guardi suggests the lagoon with dashes: a gondola is three strokes, a palace is a wash of pink. Stand close and it's chaos; stand back and it's Venice in a dream. He painted the city the way memory keeps it.

name: Pietro Longhi
teaser: The Venetian painter of everyday gossip — his small scenes of gambling salons, dressing rooms, coffee houses, and carnival visits are a documentary of 18th-century Venice between the grand tours. He painted the city's private life.

exploreAction.targetName: The Rhinoceros (1751) or The Visit
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Rhinoceros: a real rhinoceros exhibited in Venice draws a crowd of masked nobles and a frightened child. Longhi recorded the city's fads and follies with a gentle, amused eye. His little scenes are a time machine into Venice's parlors.

name: Rosalba Carriera
teaser: The Venetian pastel portraitist who made Europe fall in love with soft powder portraits — she was the most famous woman artist of the 18th century, and her pastel of a laughing girl is one of the most reproduced images of the Rococo.

exploreAction.targetName: A Young Lady with a Parrot or the pastel self-portraits
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the texture: pastel on paper gives skin a powdery softness oils can't match. Carriera's sitters glow — lips, eyes, and silk all blurred at the edges. She was elected to academies across Europe and became the favorite of the Sun King's court.

name: Francesco Solimena
teaser: The Neapolitan painter of dramatic light and enormous altarpieces — his swirling compositions of saints and allegories made Naples the second capital of Baroque painting. His studio trained half of southern Italy's artists.

exploreAction.targetName: The Expulsion of Heliodorus or the Allegory of the Kingdom
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the theatrical lighting: figures tumble through shafts of light like actors in a chapel drama. Solimena's compositions spiral — your eye climbs through them. He was the last great Neapolitan master before the city's art faded.

name: Luca Giordano
teaser: The Neapolitan painter called 'Luca Fa Presto' (Luca works fast) — he painted with a speed that amazed Europe, decorating palaces in Madrid, Florence, and Naples with ceilings of swirling color. He is the great popularizer of the Baroque.

exploreAction.targetName: The Triumph of the Medici ceiling (Palazzo Medici Riccardi) — look up
exploreAction.instruction: Tilt your head back: the Medici court floats in a heaven of clouds, gods, and golden light. Look at the energy — Giordano's brushwork is fast and confident, and it doesn't hide it. He took the grandeur of the Roman Baroque and made it portable.

name: Salvator Rosa
teaser: The Neapolitan rebel painter who made wilderness fashionable — his bandits, precipices, and stormy landscapes replaced polite Arcadia with savage nature. He was also a poet, actor, and satirist who quarreled with everyone.

exploreAction.targetName: Landscape with Bandits or the Ladder of Life
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the wildness: jagged rocks, twisted trees, and tiny bandits lurking — the 'sublime' before anyone named it. English tourists flocked to buy his dark landscapes. Then his allegory The Ladder of Life: babies, soldiers, scholars, and skulls climbing toward oblivion. A cynic's masterpiece.

name: Mattia Preti
teaser: The Calabrian painter of Caravaggio's shadow — his muscular saints and martyrs are lit with hard, dramatic light, and his painted ceiling of the life of St. John in Malta is one of the great fresco cycles of the century. He was a knight of Malta.

exploreAction.targetName: The ceiling of St. John's Co-Cathedral (Valletta) — look up
exploreAction.instruction: Lie back or crane your neck: the entire barrel vault is painted with scenes from the life of St. John, figures bursting through painted frames. Look at the tenebrism — deep shadow, sudden light, violence in holiness. Preti painted for knights, and it shows.

name: Jusepe de Ribera
teaser: The Spanish painter who worked in Naples and painted saints with wrinkles, filth, and ecstasy — his 'lo Spagnoletto' style of tenebrism and truthfulness made him the most influential painter in southern Italy. His martyrdom scenes are brutal and radiant.

exploreAction.targetName: The Martyrdom of Saint Bartholomew or the Clubfooted Boy
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the Clubfooted Boy first: a smiling, ragged boy with a clubfoot holds a piece of paper that says 'give me alms for the love of God.' No halo, no allegory — just a real child, painted with dignity. Ribera found holiness in the streets.

name: Luis de Morales
teaser: The Spanish painter of the sorrowful Virgin called 'El Divino' — his weeping Madonnas with elongated faces and emaciated Christs were so loved that he could barely keep up with demand. He painted suffering with a sweetness that made it bearable.

exploreAction.targetName: The Virgin of Sorrows or Ecce Homo (Prado) — the tears
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the restraint: a pale face, downcast eyes, a single tear catching light. Morales stripped his paintings to a face and a moment. His style — half-icon, half-portrait — made him the most popular painter in 16th-century Extremadura.

name: Alejo Fernández
teaser: The Seville painter who documented the arrival of the Americas — his Virgin of the Navigators shows Columbus, explorers, and conquerors kneeling beneath a Madonna who shelters the Spanish ships and the newly 'discovered' world.

exploreAction.targetName: The Virgin of the Navigators (Archivo de Indias, Seville) — the ships
exploreAction.instruction: The Madonna spreads her cloak over caravels, explorers, and a map of the Indies — the first painting of the age of conquest. Look at the faces: Columbus, Cortés, and the Pizarros kneel in prayer. History as devotion, painted in Seville while it was still happening.

name: Juan Sánchez Cotán
teaser: The Spanish still-life pioneer who hung vegetables and fruit in a dark window against a black void — his bodegones are so austere and precise they feel metaphysical. He later entered a Carthusian monastery and painted it as his last act.

exploreAction.targetName: Still Life with Game Fowl or Quince, Cabbage, Melon and Cucumber (San Diego)
exploreAction.instruction: A quince, a cabbage, a melon, and a cucumber hang or sit in a black window, each rendered with breathtaking exactness. Look at the space between them — that emptiness is the real subject. Cotán turned groceries into icons; Caravaggio learned from the idea.

name: Luis Egidio Meléndez
teaser: The Spanish still-life master whose kitchen tables glow — his arrangements of bread, figs, jugs, and fish are painted with a realism so rich they seem edible. He died poor and unknown; today he's considered Spain's greatest still-life painter.

exploreAction.targetName: Still Life with Watermelon and Pears or the bread and figs (Prado)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the light on the watermelon: the pink flesh seems wet, the rind green and cool. Meléndez painted food the way portraitists paint people — each piece an individual. He spent his life poor, fighting for recognition. The kitchen table was his kingdom.

name: Claudio Coello
teaser: The last great painter of the Spanish court — his enormous Sagrada Forma in the Escorial shows a kneeling Charles II before a jewelled monstrance, with the royal court and a self-portrait packed into a candlelit illusion of space.

exploreAction.targetName: The Sagrada Forma (El Escorial) — the illusion
exploreAction.instruction: The painting pretends to be an open room: arches, courtiers, a kneeling king, and Coello himself at the edge. Look at how the painted architecture matches the real chapel it hangs in — a trompe-l'oeil that makes you forget it's flat. Velázquez's last true heir.
